passage: The Ernakulam platform was roaring, the Chennai Mail was due out in five minutes, and Francis had to shout. 'Samir! Thank you. For Ammachi's house. Really.' Samir was already shaking his head. 'It was nothing, man. Just some painting.' It had not been nothing. It had been three weekends after the floods, scraping mud off the walls, rewiring the kitchen, driving two hours each way and sleeping on a mat. Francis grabbed his arm as the whistle went. 'Stop. Listen. Three weekends. You rewired the kitchen. Ammachi cried when the lights came on. That's not nothing, and you don't get to make it nothing.' Samir opened his mouth, then closed it. The train jolted. 'Okay,' he said at last. 'Okay. You're welcome.' Francis let go and jumped aboard, leaving the words with him.

qa.q: How many weekends did Samir spend on Ammachi's house?
qa.a: Samir spent three weekends on Ammachi's house.

qa.q: Why might Samir keep calling the work 'nothing'?
qa.a: Accepting thanks may feel awkward or boastful to Samir, and shrinking the work spares him from feeling how much it mattered.

qa.q: What made Francis's response work in only a few seconds?
qa.a: Francis named the specific effort, three weekends and the kitchen, and its effect on Ammachi, then refused to let it be erased, so the thanks had to land.

qa.q: How might Ammachi feel if she heard Samir call the work 'nothing'?
qa.a: Ammachi might feel a little hurt, since the lights coming on meant so much to her; for her, those weekends gave back a home.

grounding: Shows a friend on a noisy platform who hears another brush off thanks as nothing, and quickly names the real effort and lets the thanks stay.

passage: In the Gurgaon office canteen, the team lead had just thanked Parul in front of everyone for rebuilding the client presentation overnight. 'Oh, it was nothing,' Parul said, and changed the subject to the dal. Harish, who had seen her online at 2 a.m. on the office tracker, waited till the others left. 'Can I say something?' 'If it's about the slides, don't.' 'It's about the slides. You redid forty of them. You fixed the numbers finance got wrong. You came in at nine anyway.' Parul shrugged. 'Anyone would have.' 'Nobody else did.' He didn't push further. He just said, 'It was a lot of work, and it saved the pitch. That's all.' Parul stirred her tea for a long moment. 'Thanks,' she said quietly, and for once she didn't add 'but'.

qa.q: How many slides did Parul redo?
qa.a: Parul redid forty of them.

qa.q: What might Parul be feeling when she changes the subject to the dal?
qa.a: Parul seems uncomfortable with praise, perhaps feeling that accepting it would be showing off or undeserved, so she moves the attention away fast.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped the words stay?
qa.a: Harish listed the concrete effort and its result, then stopped pushing, so Parul had room to take in the thanks without arguing.

qa.q: How might the team lead feel if Parul keeps saying 'it was nothing'?
qa.a: The team lead might feel the thanks bounce off, and could underestimate how much work Parul does, which isn't fair to her.

grounding: Shows a colleague who watches a friend brush off thanks as nothing, and gently names the effort until she accepts it.

passage:
'You were incredible,' Pallavi said backstage at the community hall, still holding the marigolds.
'Please. I missed a step in the second piece.'
'Nobody saw.'
'I saw. And the lights did half the work.'
'The lights didn't practise at six every morning for a year.'
Himani laughed and started untying her ankle bells. 'It's just a small show, Pallu.'
'Three hundred people came. Your guru cried.'
'She cries at everything.'
'Himani.' Pallavi sat down on the costume trunk. 'I'm going to say one thing and you're not allowed to argue. A year of six a.m. That's what I watched tonight. That's all.'
Himani's hands stopped on the bells. For a second she looked as if she might say 'but'. Then she took the marigolds. 'Thank you,' she said. 'It was a lot of mornings.'

qa.q: How long had Himani practised at six every morning?
qa.a: Himani practised at six every morning for a year.

qa.q: Why does Himani point to the missed step and the lights?
qa.a: Taking the praise may feel risky or proud to Himani, so she finds reasons it doesn't really count, which keeps her from feeling the success.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation?
qa.a: Pallavi asked for one sentence without argument and named the year of six a.m. practice, which let Himani accept the thanks and admit, 'It was a lot of mornings.'

qa.q: How might Himani's guru feel hearing the show called 'just a small show'?
qa.a: The guru might feel a little hurt, having watched the year of effort and cried at the result; for the guru it was clearly something big.

grounding: Shows a friend backstage who hears a dancer wave away praise, names the year of early practice, and lets the thanks stay.

passage:
I'm Wasim. When my father was in hospital last winter, my friend Devika did something I still can't get over. She took over my sister's wedding preparations for a whole month: forty phone calls to caterers, two trips to Lucknow for the lehenga, a spreadsheet for the guest list that my entire family still uses.

At the wedding I tried to thank her. She laughed. "Arre, it was nothing. Anyone would have done it."

The old me would have argued. "No, really, it was huge!" and she'd have said "no, no," and we'd have gone round and round till the thanks disappeared.

This time I just said it plainly. "Devika, it was forty calls and two trips to Lucknow while you had your own job. That's a lot. Thank you." And then I stopped talking.

She opened her mouth, then closed it. She looked at the mehendi on her hands for a while.

"Okay," she said quietly. "You're welcome."

qa.q: How many phone calls did Devika make to caterers?
qa.a: Forty phone calls.

qa.q: What might Devika have been feeling when she looked at the mehendi on her hands for a while?
qa.a: She may have felt awkward and a little moved, not used to having her effort named so clearly. Being unable to wave it away probably made the thanks land.

qa.q: Why did stopping talking after the thank-you work better than arguing?
qa.a: Arguing would have started the usual back-and-forth that made the thanks disappear. Naming the effort once and then staying quiet let the words stay with Devika.

qa.q: How did Devika's help affect Wasim's family, beyond the wedding day?
qa.a: The whole family still uses her guest-list spreadsheet, and her help carried them through while Wasim's father was in hospital. That is why the thanks mattered so much to Wasim.

grounding: Wasim watches a friend wave away thanks as nothing, then names exactly how much effort she gave and lets the words stay.

passage:
Coordinator's note, animal shelter, Sunday evening

Today's adoption day placed nine dogs, our best ever. Lakshmi, one of our volunteers and a friend of mine since college, organised almost all of it: posters, the vet table, the forms, the volunteer rota. She was here at six this morning.

When the director thanked her at the end in front of everyone, Lakshmi said, "Oh, it's nothing. Everyone helped." She said something similar to three adopting families.

Afterwards, while we were rolling up mats, I said to her, "Lakshmi, you made the rota for twenty people, you came at six, and nine dogs went home. That took real effort. Thank you." I didn't add anything, and I didn't let her change the subject for a moment.

She went quiet. Then she said, "It did take a lot." She sounded surprised hearing herself say it.

Next step: I'll put her name on the thank-you board this week, and ask her to lead the next adoption day.

— Sangeeta

qa.q: How many dogs were placed at today's adoption day?
qa.a: Nine dogs.

qa.q: What does Lakshmi saying "It did take a lot" and sounding surprised suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she rarely lets herself admit her own effort, and hearing Sangeeta name it clearly let her see it too. The surprise shows how unusual it was for her to accept the praise.

qa.q: What made Sangeeta's thanks different from the director's?
qa.a: Sangeeta named specific efforts, the rota for twenty, arriving at six and nine dogs going home, and then stopped without letting the subject change. That made it hard for Lakshmi to wave away.

qa.q: How might the three adopting families feel about Lakshmi, even if she said it was nothing?
qa.a: They probably felt grateful and saw her as the one who made the day work. Their thanks was real even when Lakshmi brushed it off.

grounding: A friend who coordinates volunteers notes a young woman deflecting praise as nothing, then names her specific effort and lets the thanks stay.
